promptText: Which statement correctly distinguishes `interface` from `type` in TypeScript?
options: interface supports declaration merging (the same name can be declared twice to merge members); type cannot represent unions but interface can
interface supports declaration merging; type can express unions, tuples, and primitives that interface cannot represent at all
type and interface are fully interchangeable in every scenario with no functional differences
interface can express union types but type cannot support object shapes
explanation: Interfaces support declaration merging (repeating the name merges members) and read naturally for object/class contracts, but they cannot alias a union, tuple, or primitive — only `type` can do that.

promptText: What is the key safety difference between `unknown` and `any`?
options: any requires narrowing before use; unknown allows any operation immediately
unknown is assignable to any other type; any is not
unknown can have a value assigned TO it from anything, but you must narrow it before using it in any way; any disables type checking entirely, letting you use it however you like with no safety
There is no real difference; unknown is simply the deprecated name for any
explanation: Both accept any value being assigned to them, but unknown forces you to narrow (via typeof, instanceof, a type guard, etc.) before you can do anything with it, while any bypasses type checking completely and lets unsafe operations through silently.

promptText: Why does `const state = { status: "loading" }` fail to narrow correctly in a discriminated union, while `{ status: "loading" } as const` works?
options: as const has no actual effect on typing; it only affects runtime behavior
Without as const, the status property widens to the general type `string`, which breaks discriminant narrowing; as const freezes it to the literal type "loading" that a discriminated union needs
as const converts the object into a class instance
as const is required only for arrays, not objects
explanation: By default, TypeScript widens a property's literal value to its general type (string, number, etc.) when inferring an object's type; as const locks every property to its exact literal, readonly form, which is required for a field to work as a discriminant.

promptText: Why would typing a `children` prop as `ReactElement` instead of `ReactNode` be a mistake for a generic container component?
options: ReactElement is deprecated and no longer exists in React 18+
ReactElement only accepts a single JSX element, rejecting valid children like plain strings, numbers, arrays, or null that ReactNode (the broadest "anything renderable" type) correctly allows
ReactElement requires a `key` prop on every child
ReactNode can only be used for class components, not function components
explanation: ReactNode is the union of everything React can actually render — elements, strings, numbers, arrays, booleans, null, undefined — while ReactElement narrowly means a single JSX element, which would incorrectly reject a component receiving plain text or a fragment as children.

promptText: What does the utility type `Partial<T>` do?
options: It makes every property of T optional, which is why it's commonly used for update/patch payloads
It removes all optional properties from T, making everything required
It creates a readonly version of T with no other changes
It picks only the first property of T
explanation: Partial<T> is a mapped type equivalent to `{ [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }` — it makes every property optional, which is exactly the shape needed for a partial update object like a form patch.

promptText: In a switch statement over a discriminated union, why does assigning the switch's default-branch value to a variable typed `never` help catch bugs?
options: never causes the code to throw at compile time regardless of correctness

If every union member was already handled in earlier cases, the value remaining in the default branch is genuinely narrowed to `never`, so the assignment compiles; if a new union member is added later and left unhandled, that assignment becomes a compile error, catching the gap immediately
never is just a stylistic alias for `any` used for documentation purposes
never only works with number-based discriminants, not string literals
explanation: This is the exhaustiveness-check idiom: TypeScript narrows the switch subject to `never` in the default branch only if every possible member was already handled above; adding a new union variant without updating the switch breaks that assumption and fails to compile at exactly that spot.

promptText: Why is `inputRef.current` typed as `HTMLInputElement | null` when you declare `useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null)` and attach it to a JSX `ref` attribute, forcing you to write `inputRef.current?.focus()`?
options: TypeScript always adds `| null` to every generic type regardless of context

The ref isn't populated until after the component commits and the DOM element mounts, so during earlier code paths (or before mount) `.current` is genuinely null — the nullable type reflects that real runtime possibility
This only happens due to a TypeScript compiler bug in older versions
HTMLInputElement always includes null as one of its possible runtime values
explanation: A DOM ref starts as null and is only set once React commits the element to the DOM; the type accurately reflects that the element may not be attached yet at the point your code runs, which is why an optional-chaining guard is required.

promptText: A custom hook does `return [value, setValue];` without any annotation. Why does destructuring the result sometimes give both positions a union type instead of preserving their individual types?
options: TypeScript infers the return as an array type like `Array<value | setValue>`, widening the tuple to an array union unless you add an explicit tuple return type or append `as const`
Arrays in TypeScript can never hold values of two different types
This only happens if the hook is declared with `function*` (a generator)
Destructuring always discards type information regardless of the source type
explanation: Without an explicit tuple annotation, TypeScript infers a plain array literal's type as the union of all its element types, losing per-position typing; adding `as const` or an explicit `[T1, T2]` return type annotation fixes this by preserving each slot's specific type.

promptText: What safety guarantee does `Record<Theme, string>` (where Theme is a literal union like "light" | "dark") give you that `Record<string, string>` does not?
options: Record<Theme, string> is faster to type-check

With a literal union key, TypeScript forces every key to be present — omitting one is a compile error — and rejects unknown keys; with `string`, any key (including a typo) silently compiles with no exhaustiveness guarantee at all
Record<string, string> automatically validates keys at runtime
There is no actual difference; both behave identically
explanation: When K is a literal union, Record<K, V> requires every member to be present as a key, catching missing entries and typos at compile time; widening K to plain `string` turns it into an open-ended dictionary with no such exhaustiveness or typo protection.

promptText: Why would using `Omit` to try to remove one variant from a discriminated union type produce confusing or incorrect results?
options: Omit and Pick operate on the keys of a single object type; they cannot remove or select whole members of a union — that's the job of Exclude and Extract, which operate on union members directly
Omit is only usable on interfaces, never on type aliases
Omit silently converts the union into an intersection type
There is no difference; Omit works identically to Exclude for unions
explanation: Pick and Omit work on an object type's own property keys, not on which branch of a union you're in; to remove or select entire variants of a union you need Exclude<T, U> / Extract<T, U>, which distribute over the union's members.

promptText: Why should a generic constraint like `<T extends { label: string }>` be as narrow as possible rather than over-constraining the type parameter?
options: Overly narrow constraints always cause a compiler crash

A constraint should require exactly the shape the function's body actually needs — an over-constrained generic parameter rejects otherwise-valid callers whose objects have the required field plus extra properties the function doesn't touch
TypeScript ignores constraints wider than one property anyway
Generic constraints have no effect on which callers are accepted, only on IDE autocomplete
explanation: A constraint should express the minimum shape the function genuinely needs; making it broader (e.g. requiring a whole specific interface) than what the function body actually accesses needlessly rejects valid callers whose objects happen to have extra unrelated properties.

promptText: When typing `React.forwardRef<HandleType, PropsType>(...)`, what is the counterintuitive detail about the order of the two generic type arguments?
options: The ref/element type comes first, then the props type — reversed from how most engineers intuitively expect to write props-then-ref
Only the props type is ever specified; the ref type is always inferred automatically
forwardRef requires exactly three type arguments, not two
The order doesn't matter since TypeScript treats them as an unordered set
explanation: forwardRef's signature is <ElementType, PropsType>, i.e. the ref's target type comes first and props come second — the reverse of the order most people expect, and a very commonly missed detail.

promptText: Why does `type MyExclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T;` correctly filter members out of a union, while wrapping the check as `type NonDist<T,U> = [T] extends [U] ? never : T;` does not filter per-member?
options: Wrapping in a tuple has no effect; both forms behave identically in all TypeScript versions

When the checked type is a "naked" type parameter, TypeScript distributes the conditional over each member of a union separately and unions the results together; wrapping it in a tuple `[T]` makes it no longer naked, which suppresses that distribution and checks the whole union as one unit instead
Tuples are only used for arrays, so this syntax is actually invalid
Distribution only happens for conditional types with more than two branches
explanation: A naked type parameter directly compared in a conditional type triggers distribution over unions — this is exactly the mechanism behind Exclude/Extract/NonNullable. Wrapping either side in a one-element tuple removes the 'naked' condition, so the whole union is evaluated as a single unit instead of member-by-member.

promptText: Given `const { status, data } = state;` followed by `if (status === "success") { /* use data */ }`, why does TypeScript still treat `data` as possibly undefined inside that branch, even though narrowing `state.status` directly would have worked?
options: TypeScript's control flow analysis tracks narrowing against the specific expression checked (e.g. `state.status`), not against independently-destructured local bindings; once destructured into separate variables before the check, there's no remembered relationship between `status` and `data` for the narrowing to transfer through
Destructuring always erases all type information from an object
This is a TypeScript compiler bug that has no workaround
Only class instances support this kind of narrowing, not plain objects
explanation: Control flow narrowing is tied to the exact expression you checked. Checking `state.status === "success"` narrows `state` (and things read from it afterward), but if you destructure `status` and `data` into independent local variables BEFORE the check, TypeScript has no way to relate the narrowed `status` back to `data` — the fix is to narrow first, then destructure inside the branch.

promptText: Why would a codebase introduce branded types like `type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: "UserId" }` instead of just using `string` for every id?
options: Branded types make the runtime value more compact in memory

TypeScript's structural typing means a plain `string` can be passed anywhere a UserId is expected, silently allowing an OrderId (also a string) to be mixed up with a UserId at a call site; branding creates a phantom, compile-time-only marker that makes the two types mutually incompatible despite an identical runtime representation
Branded types cause a runtime TypeError automatically if the wrong id is passed
This technique is only useful for numeric ids, not string ids
explanation: Because TypeScript compares types structurally, two type aliases that both resolve to `string` are freely interchangeable, which lets bugs like passing an orderId where a userId is expected go uncaught; a branded type adds a phantom property that exists only in the type system, making the two nominally distinct even though both compile down to plain strings at runtime.
